task_reconstruction.objective: Estimate dragon traits, ecological effects, energy expenditure and intake, three-dragon area, community support under varying assistance, climate effects, migration advice, and a real-world model transfer.
inputs: official hatch and one-year anchors plus fictional size evidence
allometric coefficients, prey populations, masses, reproduction entries, three proxy regions, area, and mortality assumptions
task_reconstruction.decision: Advise whether and how the three dragons can survive in warm temperate, hot arid, and arctic settings without overstating deterministic proxy simulations.

contributions.summary: Converts sparse fictional size evidence into a logistic/cubic state-based growth interface.
Applies a curved temperature-aware allometric law to an extremely large fictional animal.
Builds a normalized asymmetric prey-size preference density.
Uses prey-mass density to control realized intake through a fitted scarcity exponent.
Connects prey allocation, dragon mass, prey reproduction, and starvation events in a multi-species simulation.
Runs common dynamics on New Zealand, Western Sahara, and Alaska prey ledgers.
Uses nested area sweeps to search for an arctic survival transition.

edges.handoff: Cubic mass calibration and aL^3 define the growth state scale.
Unrestricted daily mass gain m_D' enters allocated prey demand.
Basal metabolic rate B enters the printed maintenance-demand term.
Prey-size preference weights allocate demand across species.
Scarcity exponent attenuates demand as total prey mass falls.
The Lotka-Volterra scaffold motivates coupled prey and predator dynamics.
Allocated prey masses sum into the dragon mass balance.
Species-specific eaten mass becomes prey removal.
Dragon mass history is evaluated by the peak-relative starvation event.
Prey collapse drives the starvation event through reduced consumption.
Country-to-region scaling supplies prey-mass density for scarcity.
Scenario tables initialize each prey population.
Dragon trajectories provide survival outcomes for the area sweep.
The death event converts each area run into a three-dragon outcome.

assumptions.summary: Television continuity is selected when it conflicts with the books.
Magic is allowed to absorb unexplained physical discrepancies.
Dragons can continue growing when resources permit.
Dragon ages are uniformly distributed for population reasoning.
Relative prey mass and population density are treated as the only hunting-preference variables.
Drogon is treated as the maximum-resource growth envelope.
Only dragon-prey interactions enter the ecological system.
Prey communities begin near steady equilibrium.
A dragon dies at 60 percent of its own historical peak mass.
Food conversion uses 90 percent efficiency and 2500 kcal/kg for all meat.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: The growth ledger includes age, height, wingspan, mass, and reported standard deviations, but its television/image extraction procedure is incomplete.
The fitted height-to-mass coefficient is a=0.01134408 and the unrounded wingspan-to-height conversion is retained only implicitly.
The warm-temperate table combines five New Zealand livestock and wildlife categories.
The hot-arid table contains five Western Sahara proxy species and is explicitly labeled as highly estimated.
The arctic table contains eleven Alaska prey species and is more diverse than the other two scenario ledgers.
All region populations are treated as uniformly distributed so the scenario area controls local initial abundance linearly.
The scarcity calibration data are selected simulation outputs rather than independently observed density-intake pairs.
The bibliography provides only sparse row-level provenance for the numerous population, mass, reproduction, physiology, and physical-bound inputs.

verification.summary: Using the unrounded wingspan conversion gives 2520.5*(64/240)=672.1333 in and m=3,444,574.5 kg, reproducing the letter's current Drogon mass.
Using the rounded 672 in height instead gives 3,442,525.0 kg, so the letter retained hidden precision not shown in the body prose.
The logistic/cubic interface implies M_inf=aL^3=6,813,346.7 kg, proving that the fitted unrestricted curve has a finite mass asymptote.
Cubic transfer with the printed 76/61 length ratio gives Balerion about 6,657,764 kg, consistent only at the paper's stated rough precision.
The state-based gain peaks at m=(3/4)^3 M_inf=2,874,381 kg with about 4,203.7 kg/day; at the letter's Drogon mass it is about 4,097.9 kg/day.
At T=310 K the printed base-10 allometry gives about 2.00 kW and 18.4 kg/day food after conversion, far below the letter.
Interpreting the same coefficient formula with natural logs gives about 585 kW and 5,373 kg/day; the letter's 5,392 kg/day corresponds to T near 310.071 K.
Direct integration gives A=0.897621656, agreeing with the printed 0.8976 normalization constant.
The normalized preference has p(0.5)=0.0714, p(1)=0.8976, p(2)=0.2914, and p(3)=0.00997, retaining about 0.2 percent probability mass beyond x=3.
Changing the scarcity density unit from kg/km2 to the equivalent kg/m2 changes sf by about 354.8 times, demonstrating that alpha is unit-bound.
When prey is abundant and the allocation weights sum to one, Equations 7-8 yield dm/dt=m_D'/0.9, exceeding the declared unrestricted maximum by 11.1 percent.

The printed three climate tables and uniform area scaling reproduce initial prey masses near 23.94 million kg for NZ 600 km2, 361,320 kg for arid 80,000 km2, and 3.827 million kg for Alaska 27,300 km2.

results_trace.summary: The growth fit establishes a finite single-dragon mass scale near 6.813 million kg despite the paper's indefinite-growth rhetoric.
The temperate 600 km2 run starts three hatchlings and keeps all three alive through the displayed horizon.
At 600 km2 the three dragons peak collectively near 6.5 million kg and settle near 4.4 million kg while cattle disappear and deer, sheep, and fur seals remain.
At 570 km2 Viserion dies after roughly 11,000 days and the other two later starve on the same day.
At arid 80,000 km2 one dragon dies near day 1,450 and two remain near a combined 200,000 kg, with Barbary sheep dominating the response.
At arctic 27,300 km2 one dragon dies near day 4,800 and two approach about 270,000 kg combined.
At arctic 400 km2 all three quickly starve under the death rule; disabling death exposes damped mass oscillations rather than a survival conclusion.
The no-death 400 km2 diagnostic leaves long-run moose extinction unresolved at the plotted horizon.
The coarse and refined area mosaics are intended to locate a nonlinear arctic survival transition.
The refined text claims 27,100 km2 for three dragons, but this is internally contradicted by mortality at 27,300 km2.
The Conclusion's 570, 110,000, and 42,000 km2 headlines are not consistently bound to the displayed scenario trajectories.
The letter translates the hidden natural-log allometry route into about 5,392 kg/day for a 3.445 million kg Drogon.

visualization_observations.summary: Maps assumptions, dragon characteristics, metabolism, biased hunting, the ODE model, climate scenarios, sensitivity, and conclusions into the paper's planned dependency chain.
Collects eight narrative observations with height, wingspan, mass, and three standard-deviation columns for growth calibration.
Uses Aegon's stated height as an image ruler to infer Balerion's height and length before cubic mass transfer.
Displays a peak at prey-to-dragon mass ratio one, a narrow small-prey tail, and a broad decaying large-prey tail.
Lists New Zealand livestock and wildlife populations, average masses, and offspring per female per year.
Shows the coupled prey-mass traces, collective dragon mass, and three-dragon survival under the larger temperate area.
Shows one death after roughly 11,000 days followed by recovery and final starvation of the remaining two dragons.
Records five Western Sahara proxy species while the prose explicitly flags the population data as highly estimated.
Shows one dragon death and a two-dragon equilibrium driven mainly by Barbary sheep consumption.
Lists eleven Alaska prey species with population, average mass, and offspring inputs.
Shows a collective peak, moose/caribou decline, one dragon death near day 4,800, and a two-dragon endpoint.
Contrasts rapid starvation and scarce-prey trajectories at very small arctic areas.
Removes the starvation event to expose damped dragon-mass oscillations and unresolved long-run moose behavior.
Places 20,000-30,000 km2 runs in a multi-panel grid to locate a survival transition at 1,000 km2 resolution.
Places 27,000-28,000 km2 runs at 100 km2 resolution and supports the paper's 27,100 km2 claim.
Draws unlabeled supply and demand lines to argue for a finite growth limit.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: J: A parallel climate headline is judge-friendly only when all values use the same survival definition and entity level.
C: The logic diagram makes a complex coupled model navigable, but its omitted official community output remains visible in a requirement trace.
J: A near-threshold pair is memorable evidence when the successful and unsuccessful sides are labeled correctly and reconciled with the headline.
C: Nested refinement is a useful visual strategy, but contradictory brackets and an unstated decision rule undermine the claimed threshold.
J: Stakeholder advice should translate the same validated scenario ledger rather than introduce a new adult initial state without rerunning the model.

weaknesses.summary: The Summary reports 570 km2 as the warm-temperate requirement, but the body says all three dragons eventually die at 570 km2 and survive at 600 km2.
The Summary says the warm-temperate dragons grow to 4,000,000 kg without saying collective or per-dragon, while the body reports a three-dragon collective equilibrium near 4.4 million kg.
The Summary reports an arctic requirement of 42,000 km2 and mass of 3,500,000 kg without a traceable body simulation for that pair.
The Summary calls 110,000 km2 the hot-arid requirement and 86,000 kg each, but the displayed 80,000 km2 body run supports only two dragons at about 200,000 kg combined.
The Summary gives no community-size result and no comparison across assistance levels, a central official requirement.
The four-part decomposition omits the required community-size-under-varying-assistance task rather than routing it to a model section.
The logic framework names the major mathematical modules but does not show temperature, water, flight, fire, trauma, community assistance, or migration-energy pathways.
The paper assumes television continuity overrides conflicting book material without itemizing which source facts change or how uncertainty is handled.
The paper invokes magic for physical discrepancies and later presents a physical infeasibility audit, but it never defines which claims remain subject to real physics.
The assumption that dragons grow indefinitely conflicts with the finite logistic asymptote used as the unrestricted growth curve.
Uniform ages are assumed without a lifespan, sex ratio, maturity age, or reproduction model that could support an age distribution.
The no-taste-preference assumption reduces hunting to relative mass and density, omitting habitat, defense, accessibility, season, and prey behavior.
Drogon is treated as a maximum-resource growth case from narrative access to livestock, but no intake history or uncertainty supports an upper-envelope calibration.
Dragon-dragon, prey-prey, and broader food-web interactions are excluded even though the paper later claims ecosystem stability.
Countrywide prey populations are assumed to be at steady equilibrium before dragon entry, but static counts do not identify net growth equilibrium.
The fixed 60 percent peak-mass death trigger is borrowed from a human analogy and is not calibrated to dragon age, fat reserve, or starvation duration.
The discontinuous starvation threshold controls near-area results but is not included in sensitivity analysis.
The 90 percent food efficiency and universal 2500 kcal/kg meat value are asserted without prey composition, assimilation, waste, or uncertainty evidence.
Mixed height, wingspan, and mass observations are combined without an explicit conversion ledger or covariance model.
The television-derived dimensions and their standard deviations do not document frame selection, perspective correction, annotator variability, or source images.
The Balerion illustration is treated as a scale drawing even though perspective, artistic stylization, and Aegon's pose are not propagated into uncertainty.
The Balerion cubic transfer reports roughly 6,000,000 kg but does not retain the exact Drogon mass and linear dimension bundle needed to reproduce it.
The logistic fit reports L=843.717523 and k=0.71173635 but omits t0, so Equation 1 cannot be evaluated from the paper.
The claimed chi-square fit has no statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, residual table, fitted-point list, or complete parameter vector.
The paper describes Equation 2 as a function of current mass but does not show the height-to-mass coefficient a or the units of L in that interface.
The day conversion in Equation 2 is fixed at 365 while the logistic age data and parameter units are not explicitly reconciled.
Equation 3 and its coefficient line do not state the units of M or B, despite log transforms requiring a defined reference scale.
The dragon body temperature T used in the curved allometric equation is never given.

At T=310 K the printed base-10 equation gives about 2,002 W, while the same coefficients interpreted with natural logs give about 585,411 W; the letter's 5,392 kg/day food value closely matches the natural-log route, not the printed log10 route.
The allometric regression is extrapolated far beyond observed animals without prediction intervals, alternate exponents, or sensitivity to body temperature.
The piecewise preference density is mathematically normalized by A=0.8976, but the paper does not show the integral or clarify that its support extends beyond the plotted x=3.5 range.
The prose suggests prey up to roughly three times dragon mass, but the right Gaussian has no hard cutoff and retains positive probability beyond x=3.
The two Gaussian widths and their asymmetry are chosen narratively rather than estimated from observed hunting behavior.
The preference density is not empirically calibrated to hunting observations and does not model the higher absolute cost of attacking very large prey.
The scarcity factor raises a dimensioned prey-density quantity to a noninteger power without a reference density, making alpha unit-dependent.
Scarcity parameters were selected from runs whose behavior looked expected and then fit by a power law, a circular calibration procedure the authors acknowledge.
No objective loss, labeled calibration data, holdout scenario, or confidence interval supports alpha=13.2948 and gamma=-0.425.
The Lotka-Volterra scaffold uses x and y as population states but the final system replaces the predator population with separate dragon masses without a formal derivation.
Prey natural growth is reduced to births minus deaths without sex ratio, maturity, gestation interval, density dependence, or seasonal timing.
Equation 7 adds m_D'/0.9 to 2500B even though the first term is kg/day and, with B in kcal/day and 2500 kcal/kg, the second printed product is not kg/day.
Converting BMR from kcal/day to food mass requires division by 2500 kcal/kg, not multiplication; Equation 7 has the conversion direction reversed.
Equation 8 again subtracts 2500B from consumed prey mass, so its two sides are dimensionally incompatible as printed.
Even ignoring the BMR unit problem, abundant prey makes Equations 7-8 reduce to dm_D/dt=m_D'/0.9, exceeding the declared unrestricted maximum gain by 11.1 percent.
The plotted dragon state is collective mass, while the preference ratio and 60 percent death event require per-dragon masses and peak histories; the aggregate-to-individual interface is undefined.
The temperate collective peak near 6.5 million kg is close to the 6.813 million kg single-dragon logistic asymptote, suggesting the code may apply a single-dragon cap to an aggregate state.
The letter's 5,392 kg/day food figure cannot be reproduced from the printed multiplication and therefore appears to come from a different implementation.
Equations 7-8 use basal metabolism only and omit flight, hunting, fire breathing, combat, thermoregulation, reproduction, and injury recovery.
The preference allocation denominator and initial/current prey-mass ratio have no defined behavior when a preferred species or total prey mass approaches zero.
Equation 9 treats fractional eaten mass divided by individual mass as continuous deaths, without nonnegativity events or integer handling.
The ODE solver is described only as a Python wrapper switching Adams and BDF; solver name, tolerances, Jacobian, event handling, and source code are absent.
Country-to-region population scaling is described in prose but no equation, country area, or row-by-row local initial state is published.
The New Zealand table mixes domestic livestock with wild species without modeling continued human breeding, husbandry, slaughter, imports, or land limits.
The 600 km2 run is described as a steady state without a numerical convergence criterion or horizon-sensitivity check.
The temperate body result labels 4.4 million kg as the combined mass of all three dragons, unlike the Summary and Conclusion's ambiguous entity level.
At 570 km2 one dragon dies and the remaining two later starve, so the run is evidence of insufficiency rather than the minimum supporting area claimed elsewhere.
The arid input populations are explicitly highly estimated, yet the final area and mass claims carry no uncertainty range.
The 80,000 km2 arid run ends with only two dragons; it does not directly validate the three-dragon 110,000 km2 headline.
The arid outcome is dominated by one small, guessed Barbary sheep population, making the threshold highly sensitive to an acknowledged low-quality input.
At 27,300 km2 the arctic body run loses one dragon around day 4,800 and ends with two dragons near 270,000 kg combined.
The arctic prose calls the remaining community completely stable despite continued caribou decline and without an equilibrium test.
The 400 km2 death-off experiment changes the model class by removing mortality and should be treated as a diagnostic, not survival validation.
The paper admits additional simulation is needed to know whether moose eventually go extinct, so the plotted finite-horizon behavior cannot establish long-run stability.
The generalized invasive-predator application removes discrete dragon deaths but does not add predator reproduction, mortality, age, or calibration for a real species.
The stinkbug example is an invasive prey/pest rather than an invasive apex predator and does not match the model's trophic mechanism.
The sensitivity section varies only area; it omits mortality threshold, prey data, preference, scarcity, metabolism, initial masses, and solver settings.
The refined sensitivity text claims 27,100 km2 sustains all three dragons, conflicting with the displayed 27,300 km2 run where one dragon dies.
The sensitivity mosaics do not label every panel in an ordered outcome table, state a shared horizon, or quantify the survival decision rule.
The authors acknowledge estimates and guesses in IUCN-derived population data but do not identify each guessed row or propagate the uncertainty.
The authors acknowledge omitted dragon-dragon and prey-prey interactions, which invalidates broad claims about a stable ecosystem rather than only refining them.
The self-critique of scarcity-factor manipulation gives no replacement calibration strategy or evidence collection plan.
The leg-pressure audit uses a 10^4 kg adult example, inconsistent with the million-kilogram masses used in the growth and climate results.
The wing-loading audit likewise uses 10^4 kg and cites an unresolved [?] reference, so its 500 m2 requirement is neither source-supported nor aligned with the modeled dragon.
The thermodynamic mortality argument is qualitative and does not estimate lifespan, senescence, or damage repair.
The claim that three-quarter-power maintenance demand outpaces energy supply is logically unsupported: sublinear demand alone does not exceed linearly scaling supply.
Figure 3 has no axis variables, units, functional forms, data, or fitted intersection and cannot validate the claimed energy limit.
The Conclusion reports 570 km2 as the temperate requirement despite the body showing total dragon extinction at that area.
The Conclusion reports 42,000 km2 and 3,500,000 kg for the arctic case without reconciling 27,100 and 27,300 km2 or the body endpoint near 270,000 kg.
The Conclusion reports 110,000 km2 and 86,000 kg each for the arid case without presenting the supporting three-dragon trajectory or threshold search.
The letter applies a 3,444,574 kg season-7 Drogon state to body simulations that start with three newly hatched dragons, without a matching transient rerun.
The letter's 5,392 kg/day food estimate lacks an activity multiplier, flight, combat, fire, hunting, and cold-temperature expenditure.
The letter says one temperate dragon can feed indefinitely, but the displayed temperate simulations concern three hatchlings and do not validate current-mass Drogon.
The letter warns Drogon cannot remain in the North for more than a few days, but no migration time, travel distance, flight cost, battle cost, or finite-duration simulation supports that limit.
The two-page letter gives no quantitative table comparing warm temperate, hot arid, and arctic requirements under consistent entity and time bases.
No section computes required community population, labor, supply chain, land, or infrastructure under any assistance level.
Only eight references support narrative facts, the ODE scaffold, population data, allometry, diet, and scaling; many table entries and physical claims lack row-level citations.
The unresolved [?] wing-loading citation and sparse web-source metadata prevent reliable source tracing.

independent_extensions.summary: Refit the growth curve with all parameters, residuals, uncertainty, and an explicit finite-versus-unbounded model comparison.
Rebuild metabolism with declared logarithm base, M/B/T units, temperature scenarios, activity components, and prediction intervals.
Replace the printed energy conversion with a dimensionally closed intake-assimilation-maintenance-growth ledger and test conservation.
Track three individual dragon masses and peak histories rather than mixing a collective mass curve with per-dragon preference and mortality.
Add explicit assistance levels mapping hunted fraction, supplied food, labor productivity, households, land, logistics, and infrastructure to community population.
Separate climate mechanisms through temperature, water, seasonality, prey productivity, migration duration, flight cost, and combat cost.
Run global sensitivity and uncertainty propagation over prey data, allometry, preference, scarcity, mortality, initial mass, area, and solver settings.

The Lotka-Volterra scaffold uses x and y as population states but the final system replaces the predator population with separate dragon masses without a formal derivation.
Prey natural growth is reduced to births minus deaths without sex ratio, maturity, gestation interval, density dependence, or seasonal timing.
Equation 7 adds m_D'/0.9 to 2500B even though the first term is kg/day and, with B in kcal/day and 2500 kcal/kg, the second printed product is not kg/day.
Converting BMR from kcal/day to food mass requires division by 2500 kcal/kg, not multiplication; Equation 7 has the conversion direction reversed.
Equation 8 again subtracts 2500B from consumed prey mass, so its two sides are dimensionally incompatible as printed.
Even ignoring the BMR unit problem, abundant prey makes Equations 7-8 reduce to dm_D/dt=m_D'/0.9, exceeding the declared unrestricted maximum gain by 11.1 percent.
The plotted dragon state is collective mass, while the preference ratio and 60 percent death event require per-dragon masses and peak histories; the aggregate-to-individual interface is undefined.
The temperate collective peak near 6.5 million kg is close to the 6.813 million kg single-dragon logistic asymptote, suggesting the code may apply a single-dragon cap to an aggregate state.
The letter's 5,392 kg/day food figure cannot be reproduced from the printed multiplication and therefore appears to come from a different implementation.
Equations 7-8 use basal metabolism only and omit flight, hunting, fire breathing, combat, thermoregulation, reproduction, and injury recovery.
The preference allocation denominator and initial/current prey-mass ratio have no defined behavior when a preferred species or total prey mass approaches zero.
Equation 9 treats fractional eaten mass divided by individual mass as continuous deaths, without nonnegativity events or integer handling.
The ODE solver is described only as a Python wrapper switching Adams and BDF; solver name, tolerances, Jacobian, event handling, and source code are absent.
Country-to-region population scaling is described in prose but no equation, country area, or row-by-row local initial state is published.
The New Zealand table mixes domestic livestock with wild species without modeling continued human breeding, husbandry, slaughter, imports, or land limits.
The 600 km2 run is described as a steady state without a numerical convergence criterion or horizon-sensitivity check.
The temperate body result labels 4.4 million kg as the combined mass of all three dragons, unlike the Summary and Conclusion's ambiguous entity level.
At 570 km2 one dragon dies and the remaining two later starve, so the run is evidence of insufficiency rather than the minimum supporting area claimed elsewhere.
The arid input populations are explicitly highly estimated, yet the final area and mass claims carry no uncertainty range.
The 80,000 km2 arid run ends with only two dragons; it does not directly validate the three-dragon 110,000 km2 headline.
The arid outcome is dominated by one small, guessed Barbary sheep population, making the threshold highly sensitive to an acknowledged low-quality input.
At 27,300 km2 the arctic body run loses one dragon around day 4,800 and ends with two dragons near 270,000 kg combined.
The arctic prose calls the remaining community completely stable despite continued caribou decline and without an equilibrium test.
The 400 km2 death-off experiment changes the model class by removing mortality and should be treated as a diagnostic, not survival validation.
The paper admits additional simulation is needed to know whether moose eventually go extinct, so the plotted finite-horizon behavior cannot establish long-run stability.
The generalized invasive-predator application removes discrete dragon deaths but does not add predator reproduction, mortality, age, or calibration for a real species.
The stinkbug example is an invasive prey/pest rather than an invasive apex predator and does not match the model's trophic mechanism.
The sensitivity section varies only area; it omits mortality threshold, prey data, preference, scarcity, metabolism, initial masses, and solver settings.
The refined sensitivity text claims 27,100 km2 sustains all three dragons, conflicting with the displayed 27,300 km2 run where one dragon dies.
The sensitivity mosaics do not label every panel in an ordered outcome table, state a shared horizon, or quantify the survival decision rule.
The authors acknowledge estimates and guesses in IUCN-derived population data but do not identify each guessed row or propagate the uncertainty.
The authors acknowledge omitted dragon-dragon and prey-prey interactions, which invalidates broad claims about a stable ecosystem rather than only refining them.
The self-critique of scarcity-factor manipulation gives no replacement calibration strategy or evidence collection plan.
The leg-pressure audit uses a 10^4 kg adult example, inconsistent with the million-kilogram masses used in the growth and climate results.
The wing-loading audit likewise uses 10^4 kg and cites an unresolved [?] reference, so its 500 m2 requirement is neither source-supported nor aligned with the modeled dragon.
The thermodynamic mortality argument is qualitative and does not estimate lifespan, senescence, or damage repair.
The claim that three-quarter-power maintenance demand outpaces energy supply is logically unsupported: sublinear demand alone does not exceed linearly scaling supply.
Figure 3 has no axis variables, units, functional forms, data, or fitted intersection and cannot validate the claimed energy limit.
The Conclusion reports 570 km2 as the temperate requirement despite the body showing total dragon extinction at that area.
The Conclusion reports 42,000 km2 and 3,500,000 kg for the arctic case without reconciling 27,100 and 27,300 km2 or the body endpoint near 270,000 kg.
The Conclusion reports 110,000 km2 and 86,000 kg each for the arid case without presenting the supporting three-dragon trajectory or threshold search.
The letter applies a 3,444,574 kg season-7 Drogon state to body simulations that start with three newly hatched dragons, without a matching transient rerun.
The letter's 5,392 kg/day food estimate lacks an activity multiplier, flight, combat, fire, hunting, and cold-temperature expenditure.
The letter says one temperate dragon can feed indefinitely, but the displayed temperate simulations concern three hatchlings and do not validate current-mass Drogon.
The letter warns Drogon cannot remain in the North for more than a few days, but no migration time, travel distance, flight cost, battle cost, or finite-duration simulation supports that limit.
The two-page letter gives no quantitative table comparing warm temperate, hot arid, and arctic requirements under consistent entity and time bases.
No section computes required community population, labor, supply chain, land, or infrastructure under any assistance level.
Only eight references support narrative facts, the ODE scaffold, population data, allometry, diet, and scaling; many table entries and physical claims lack row-level citations.
The unresolved [?] wing-loading citation and sparse web-source metadata prevent reliable source tracing.
